site: Workday (Copart) 'How Did You Hear About Us?' nested list; any click whose target leaves the page -- submission_guard.SubmissionGuardV0.click_was_denied, used by browser_automation._click_resiliently and interaction.click_resiliently
class: A safety check verified an action's outcome through the very object the action destroys, so a successful action was indistinguishable from a refused one and was reported as refused
symptom: Copart's required field 'How Did You Hear About Us?' stayed empty on every attempt: the agent typed 'LinkedIn' but never chose a row, and the page it left behind showed the list stuck inside the 'Campus Campaign' sub-menu. The run log carried four 'SUBMISSION_GUARD_V0_DENIED: refusing click fallback' events, each about 30 seconds after the last, and the form then refused to go on ('The field ... is required and must have a value').
root_cause: After each click the guard read its denial counter through the clicked element's own locator. In a nested prompt a click that works removes that element (the list closes, or the category row is replaced by its sub-menu), so the locator waited its full 30-second timeout for an element that no longer existed, raised, and click_was_denied took 'cannot verify' to mean 'denied'. The click that had worked was reported as failed. The nested-list walker therefore believed it was still on the top list, tried other rows from the wrong place, and left the field typed but never chosen. It is the same family as f146: a guard written for the Submit button blocked ordinary interaction clicks.
why_tests_missed: Every firewall test clicked an element that stays on the page (a Submit button that is denied, or a plain button), so the denial counter was always readable afterwards; no test clicked something that removes itself, and the click helpers were exercised only with stub locators that never detach.
fix: SubmissionGuardV0.click_frame() finds the clicked element's frame before the click, and click_was_denied() reads the denial counter from that frame, which outlives the element and answers at once. If the frame's document itself was replaced by the click, that is proof the click took effect (a refused click leaves the document as it was), so it is not a denial. A real denial is still read from the frame's counter and still stops the fallback; any other failure to read the counter still fails closed. Both copies of the click helper (browser_automation._click_resiliently and interaction.click_resiliently) pass the frame.
prevention: Verify an action's outcome through something that survives the action. Reading a result back through the element you just clicked fails exactly when the click worked best (the element is replaced or removed), and a check that treats 'could not read it' as 'refused' then turns every success of that kind into a failure. Keep a handle to the container (the frame) before acting, and treat the container changing as evidence the action had an effect. When a guard fails closed, test the fail-closed branch against actions that legitimately remove their own target, not only against the action it exists to block.
